text:
Jordan Lee: ADR-0147 review time. Main open question: do we want weighted fair queueing (WFQ-ish) across lanes/tenants, or strict priority for enterprise lane with some bounded starvation protection?

Ravi Menon: tl;dr I’m leaning strict priority between lanes (enterprise > self-serve) with explicit starvation bounds. WFQ sounds “nice” but the implementation surface gets big fast (weights, deficit accounting, per-tenant state, etc.).

Mina Haddad: +1 on keeping it simple, but we have to be careful: strict priority + retry storms = self-serve basically dead for long windows, and then we get weird feedback loops (clients hammer harder).

Sean Gallagher: from SRE angle: I’m ok with self-serve shedding during overload *as long as it’s predictable* and doesn’t take down the fleet. But we should avoid “blackout” behavior that lasts > a few minutes, otherwise we create a second incident (support + reputational).

Ethan Park: can we define what “bounded starvation” means concretely? Like “self-serve gets at least X% of admit rate when healthy capacity exists” or “at least 1 request per N ms per region”? ADR needs numbers or at least a policy mechanism.

Ravi Menon: proposal in the draft: strict priority w/ a cap: after `K` consecutive enterprise dequeues, we force one from standard lane if queue not empty. K configurable per region/cluster. Also a time-based escape hatch: if standard queue wait > `T`, allow it to jump.

Sofia Ivanova: runtime note: whatever you do, please don’t create a pattern that causes oscillation at sub-second frequency. Tail latency gets gnarly if the router flips admission rapidly while the runtime is already doing continuous batching.

Elena Popov: if we do “K consecutive” it’s easy in code. We already maintain separate queues per lane. It becomes a simple counter on the worker loop.

Allison Grant: metrics/observability: WFQ would require more per-tenant labeling if you want to prove fairness. Please don’t. Lane-level is already high-cardinality when you add `route` + `region`. A simple lane starvation counter is manageable.

Mina Haddad: I still want to sanity check tail latency impact. Strict priority can reduce enterprise p99 (good) but can increase p99 for everyone else (expected). WFQ might increase enterprise tail if we’re always servicing standard fraction.

Jordan Lee: right, the trade: we’re explicitly choosing enterprise SLO preservation over global fairness. ADR should state that.

Sean Gallagher: also call out failure modes: if the “enterprise lane” itself gets overloaded, strict priority does nothing to help. We still need admission control keyed by route/tier. Otherwise enterprise can DoS enterprise.

Ravi Menon: yep. The lane is a *routing* primitive; the gate is per-route/per-tenant. The goal is protect top enterprise routes from noisy neighbors + partial capacity loss.

Ethan Park: what about “reserved capacity”? If we do strict priority, do we also reserve a % of tokens/sec for enterprise?

Mina Haddad: the current design is “soft reservation” by having enterprise always ahead in the queue. True reservation would require either (a) separate router pools or (b) runtime-level scheduling reservation. Out of scope per program brief.

Sofia Ivanova: +1. The runtime team can expose backpressure signals (queue depth, prefill saturation), but it’s not going to do per-tier reservations in kernels this quarter.

Jordan Lee: ok, so ADR language: “strict priority across lanes at router admission; bounded starvation for lower tier to avoid complete blackout; no hard GPU reservation.”

Allison Grant: please add a requirement: export `lane_starvation_seconds{lane="standard"}` (or similar) aggregated per region, NOT per tenant. Also track `queue_wait_p99` per lane.

Elena Popov: implementation detail: if we do time-based escape hatch, we need a monotonic enqueue timestamp on requests. That’s fine.

Connor O'Brien: rollout concern: can we ship strict priority first behind a flag and keep the starvation knobs disabled by default? I’d rather we ramp in “K” once we see behavior in canary.

Sean Gallagher: I’d prefer the starvation guardrails enabled from day 1, even if conservative (like K=50). Otherwise we’ll create the very “self-serve blackout” that triggers support escalations during the first real overload.

Mina Haddad: +1, especially since we’re doing this because we’ve seen retry storms. Those are exactly when strict priority without bounds is scary.

Ravi Menon: compromise: default K=20, T=2s (for standard lane jump). We can tune in canary. Enterprise still dominates, but standard isn’t dead.

Jordan Lee: does that harm enterprise p99 meaningfully?

Sofia Ivanova: unlikely unless enterprise is right at saturation and standard is constantly queued. But if that’s true, you’re in overload anyway; the bigger lever is shedding standard earlier (429) so it doesn’t compete.

Ethan Park: important: define ordering: do we evaluate per-route throttle first, then lane queueing? I think yes: enforce quotas/rate limits at gateway, then router lane admission, then runtime.

Ravi Menon: agreed. ADR will spell out: gateway limits first; router lanes second; runtime backpressure can trigger additional shedding.

Allison Grant: and please call it “bounded starvation” not “fairness” in the ADR. “Fairness” will cause bikeshedding forever.

Jordan Lee: :thumbsup: action items: Ravi update ADR-0147 with strict priority + bounded starvation (K + T), explicitly document why not WFQ (complexity + observability/cardinality + runtime interaction), and add tail latency considerations + metrics requirements. Sean to add SRE note on support impact if blackout > N minutes.

Ravi Menon: will do. I’ll push an updated draft today and tag @Jordan Lee @Sean Gallagher for final sign-off.

Sean Gallagher: thanks. also add a line: “WFQ can be revisited once per-customer reserved capacity exists” so we don’t get asked every review.

Jordan Lee: done. marking WFQ as deferred w/ rationale.
